title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
claim: A long history is folded recurrently into a fixed-size memory, with a consistency loss tying sequential and packed processing.
layout: Top recurrence chain feeding 3 zoomed panels (a)-(c), left-to-right, dashed zoom-in
description: A wide system diagram. The top row shows archived segments S_1…S_K feeding a chain of update operators U, which turn M_0=0 into M_1 … M_K. Each M is a yellow box, each U a green circle. A recent-suffix box X_rec in orange sits at top right. A dashed line zooms from U into three rounded panels below. Panel (a) is the memory update: HSTU shared, a high-level encoder, a candidate memory, a slot-wise forget gate equation, and a norm projection. Panel (b) is stream-consistency training. It compares sequential and packed updates from M_{K-2} through shared-weight decoders and a KL loss with stop-gradient. Panel (c) is prediction: memory and recent tokens go through the shared HSTU and a decoder to the NCE loss. The total loss is at the bottom right. Colors mark shared (blue), encoder (green), and decoder (orange) components, and purple marks losses.
caption: Overview of RecMem. Top: U folds the K archived segments into a fixed-size memory state, one segment at a time. (a) In each update, the slot-wise forget gate is computed from the mask-aware mean of E(St). (b) Both branches start from the same MK−2, and the packed update uses repeated segment-local positions and a causal mask. The two final states are decoded with the same Xrec and candidates; sg denotes stop-gradient. (c) Recent tokens attend to all memory slots and causally to each other. The decoder outputs at all recent positions, Hrec, enter the NCE loss with shifted positives Y + and sampled negatives Y −; at inference, the last row of Hrec scores candidate items. Blue, green, and orange mark shared, encoder-side, and decoder-side components.
abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.
